author: Craig Barton
summary: This Tips for Teachers research summary covers John Mason's 2010 analysis of teacher questioning in the mathematics classroom, which reframes questions as arising from a shift in the teacher's own attention rather than as a neutral information-gathering tool. Mason distinguishes between controlling questions (which steer students toward a predetermined answer), genuine inquiries (which invite real mathematical thinking), and meta-questions, and warns of a specific failure mode called 'funnelling,' where a string of narrowing questions does the mathematical thinking for the student rather than prompting it. Central to his argument is the idea of a 'conjecturing atmosphere' — a classroom culture in which students feel safe proposing and revising ideas without fear of being judged for being wrong. Mason also argues that teachers should actively cultivate students' own question-generation, since a student who learns to ask their own mathematical questions has taken genuine ownership of their learning, rather than simply responding to the teacher's prompts. Barton's summary draws out Mason's warning that the pattern of questions a teacher habitually uses silently communicates their real philosophy of teaching to students, whatever the teacher intends to signal.
points: Mason distinguishes controlling questions, genuine inquiries, and meta-questions, and names 'funnelling' — a narrowing sequence of questions that does the mathematical thinking for the student — as a specific failure mode to avoid.
A 'conjecturing atmosphere,' where students feel safe proposing and revising ideas without judgment, is presented as a precondition for genuine mathematical engagement, not an optional nicety.
Questions originate from a shift in the teacher's own attention, meaning teachers who are more aware of what they're attending to can ask more deliberately effective questions.
Encouraging students to generate their own questions is framed as a marker of genuine ownership of learning, not just a nice-to-have engagement technique.

Mason's closing warning is that the pattern of questions a teacher habitually asks covertly reveals their real philosophy of teaching to students, regardless of what the teacher believes they are communicating.
quotes: Mason proposes that teacher questions often stem from a shift in the teacher's own attention, aiming to redirect student focus.
The text analyzes different types of questions, including controlling questions, genuine inquiries, and meta-questions, exploring their effectiveness and potential drawbacks like funneling.
It also emphasizes creating a conjecturing atmosphere where students feel comfortable making and revising conjectures.
Teachers should strive to create a conjecturing atmosphere in the classroom, where students feel comfortable sharing their ideas and making conjectures without fear of being judged.
When students ask their own questions, they are taking ownership of their learning.
Above all, the types of questions you ask will quickly inform your learners of what you expect of them, and covertly, of your enacted philosophy of teaching.

The key to effective questioning lies in rarely using norming and controlling questions, in using focusing questions sparingly and reflectively, and using genuine enquiry-questions as much as possible.
